5Extend it

Tools, MCP, skills: new abilities without a new model.

ⓘ Notes
Tools give it new actions, MCP plugs in tools others built, and skills give it know-how loaded on demand. All their descriptions take context.

Why it’s designed this way: Changing the model is slow and costly; manuals and hands from outside work the same day.

Stop 5 of 27 📍 App overview › Using agents › Extend it
On this page:

🧒 In plain words first

What a model knows is fixed once it is trained. The easiest way to make it do more is to hand it instruction sheets and give it “hands”, like installing apps on a phone. There are three ways: add tools one by one, plug in a whole set someone else built (MCP), or give it a pack of “how-to notes” (Skills). The cost: every instruction sheet takes up room on its “desk” (the context).

Go deeper (the full explanation)

What a model knows is fixed at training time. The cheapest way to make it do new things is to hand it manuals and hands from outside. Three ways:

  • Tools (function calling): give it a new action (check stock, send a message).
  • MCP (Model Context Protocol): plug in whole sets of tools and data others have built, through one open protocol.
  • Skills (skill packs): hand it a pack of “how to do this kind of task” instructions (scripts optional), read only when needed.

All three share one cost: their descriptions must go into the Context window before the model knows they exist.

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

A tool is an instruction sheet plus a program. The sheet tells the model “my name, what I do, what details to fill in”; when the model wants it, it writes a “request form”, the program checks it, does the real work, and reports the result back. The sheet should be easy to understand at a glance.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

A tool is two things a developer writes: a manual for the model (name, purpose, parameter format) and the program that does the work. For example: Illustrative

{
  "name": "check_stock",
  "description": "Look up the stock count of a product",
  "parameters": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": { "sku": { "type": "string" } },
    "required": ["sku"]
  }
}

When needed, the model writes text like {"name":"check_stock","arguments":{"sku":"A-102"}}; the program checks the arguments, calls the real system and sends the result back as text. Details in Tool manual (function description) and ⑤ Tool result.

Good tools: obvious names, a description that says when to use it, few parameters; keep read-only tools apart from ones that change things, and add confirmation to the latter.

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

MCP is like a standard socket: before, every AI app needed a separate plug for every tool; with a standard socket, each tool and each app does the work once and they all fit together. But plugging in an unknown plug means trusting it, so only install ones from sources you trust.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open protocol proposed in late 2024. Before it, each AI app had to integrate each tool separately (N apps × M tools); with one protocol, each side implements it once and they connect (N + M).

  • Three roles: the AI app (host) (the AI app you use) opens one MCP client per server, connected to an MCP server.
  • A server offers three kinds of things: tools (actions), resources (data to read) and prompts (ready-made templates).
  • Two ways to connect: standard input/output (stdio) when the server runs locally; HTTP when it is remote.

Safety: installing a server means trusting its code and everything it can reach, and what it returns may carry a Prompt injection. Install only trusted ones, and check the access they ask for.

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

A skill pack is like a how-to manual on a shelf: normally only its title and a one-line summary show, which takes little room; when a related job comes up, the helper takes the whole manual down and follows it, and it can include ready-made small programs.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

A skill is a folder: a SKILL.md file says how to do a kind of task, starting with a name and a one-line description; it may also hold scripts and templates.

  1. Normally: only each skill’s name and description sit in the context, a few dozen tokens each.
  2. When relevant: the agent decides a skill fits the task, then reads the full instructions and runs its scripts if needed.
ToolSkill
What it addsAn action (hands)A way of working (know-how)
Context when idleThe full manualName + description only
Who runs itThe appThe agent follows it, using existing tools
⚠️ Mix-up

🧒 In plain words first

A tool is like a screwdriver: it does one specific job. MCP is like a standard wall socket that all kinds of tools can plug into. A Skill is like a how-to manual for a kind of job, opened only when that job comes up.

In one line: a tool is one action the agent can take (a manual plus a program); MCP is the standard socket that plugs tools (and data) in, not an action itself; a Skill is written know-how for a kind of task, read in only when needed, and following it often means using tools.

🔧 Tool

  • Like: a screwdriver (hands)
  • What: a name, purpose and parameter format, plus the program that does the work
  • Who runs it: the app, with the arguments the model filled in

🔌 MCP

  • Like: a standard wall socket
  • What: an open protocol: an MCP server offers tools, resources and prompts, and any MCP-capable app can connect
  • Solves: no per-app, per-tool integration (N × M → N + M)

📦 Skills

  • Like: a how-to manual (know-how)
  • What: a folder: SKILL.md with the steps, maybe scripts and templates
  • Idle cost: only the name and a one-line description; the full text is read when needed
  • They stack: a Skill says “look it up with tool A, then change it with tool B”, and A and B arrive through an MCP server.
  • Every tool an MCP server brings keeps its manual in the context all the time; installing too many crowds the context.

🧠 Remember: a tool is a hand, MCP is the socket, a Skill is the manual.

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

Before installing an MCP server, ask a few questions as you would before letting a stranger into your home: who made it? What will it do? What of mine can it see? Will it ask me every time? Is it given as few keys as possible? Could what it reads hide bad instructions?

Go deeper (the full explanation)

The MCP specification's Security and Trust section lists three key principles: user consent and control, data privacy and tool safety. It also says the protocol itself cannot enforce them; the AI app (host) has to build the consent screens and access controls. So whether to install, and with how much access, is finally your call.

  • Is the source trusted? The spec says tool descriptions and annotations should be treated as untrusted unless they come from a trusted server. Check who publishes it and whether the code is public.
  • What will it do? Tools amount to arbitrary code execution. Read each tool it offers before you authorise it, and understand it.
  • What data can it see? The spec says a host must get your explicit consent before exposing your data to a server, and must not pass resource data elsewhere without consent.
  • Will each call ask you? The spec says a host must get explicit consent before invoking any tool. Keep the confirmation step; don't switch everything to “always allow”.
  • Is access minimal? Give it only the folders, accounts and network this job needs (see Least privilege and human confirmation).
  • Could what it reads give orders? Text in web pages, emails and documents can carry Prompt injection. A server that reads outside content shouldn't also be able to send or delete.

As a reminder, a server can offer three kinds of thing: resources (data), prompt templates and tools; see MCP server. Look at all three before installing.

Sources: MCP Specification (2025-11-25) · Security and Trust & Safety

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

Some models can be downloaded and run on your own computer, so your data never leaves the machine and it works offline. The costs: your computer’s memory limits how big a model you can run, it is usually slower than the cloud, and you must handle updates and security yourself. Running locally does not automatically mean safer.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

Open-weight models can be downloaded and run on your own computer or server. Take two widely used open-source tools (see the sources below):

  • A one-command runner: its site says it runs open models locally or in the cloud. Locally it starts a server (the docs use localhost:11434) that supports a subset of a widely used chat API, so many existing tools connect by changing one address.
  • A C/C++ inference library: plain C/C++ with minimal setup; uses the GGUF file format; supports 1.5- to 8-bit integer quantisation for speed and lower memory; CPU+GPU hybrid inference partially accelerates models larger than total VRAM.
Good reasons to go localData must not leave the machine; it must work offline; you want to control the version yourself.
What it costsModel size is limited by RAM/VRAM; speed is usually below big cloud clusters; you handle updates and patches yourself.

Whether it fits comes down to two sums: the weights themselves (Quantization shrinks them) and the KV cache, which grows with long chats. In “MoE & efficiency”, the KV-cache memory calculator and the quantisation lab let you work it out.

Note: “local is always safer” is not true. Model files and tools must still come from trusted sources, and access still needs limits.

Sources: Runner home page · Runner docs · API compatibility · ggml-org inference library README

🧪 How much context do the manuals take?

🧒 In plain words first

The more extensions you install, the more “desk” their instruction sheets take. Compare “put everything in” with “fetch when needed” and see how much room each takes (the token counts are illustrative).

ⓘ All token counts are illustrative round numbers; real ones depend on the model and how descriptions are written.

Why it’s built this way:
  • Every extension must introduce itself first, in the context; the more you install, the more crowded it gets.
  • Loading on demand (name and one line first, full text when used) is how skills and many tool systems save room.



👀 Try this:
  • Pick 30, put everything in, and see how much the manuals take
  • Switch to “load on demand” and compare
  • With on-demand loading, tap “Call a tool once” and see when the full manual comes in
